result:
The Permission to Wander

There is a particular kind of silence that arrives when someone says, *write about whatever you want*. It is not empty. It is the silence of a field just after a gate has been left open. You stand at the edge, and for a moment the absence of direction feels almost vertiginous.

When I was a child, I used to go walking without a destination. Not to get anywhere, not to exercise, not to clear my head. Just to see what the world would offer if I didn’t ask it for anything specific. I would follow the crooked line of a fence, or the smell of someone’s woodstove, or a stray cat that seemed to know exactly where it was going. The point was never arrival. The point was the permission to be curious.

I think we lose that permission as adults. We start to believe that every hour must be spent productively, every sentence must advance an argument, every walk must have a step count. But there is a quiet rebellion in writing without a plan. It says: I trust my mind enough to let it wander. I trust that even in the detours, something true might surface.

So here I am, writing freely, and what surfaces is this: the smell of rain on warm pavement, the sound of a screen door closing in summer, the particular loneliness of a lit window seen from a passing train. These are not arguments. They are not even stories. They are just impressions, but they matter to me. They are the unedited texture of being alive.

Maybe the real gift of “whatever you want” is not the freedom to choose a topic, but the freedom to stop performing. To write without a thesis, without an audience looking over your shoulder, without the need to be clever or correct. To simply let the mind lean out the window and watch the landscape go by.

So I will keep writing until the impulse softens. Until the sentences stop arriving. And when they do, I will not call it failure. I will call it the end of a walk I didn’t know I needed to take.
